descriptor.en: Information Technology: AI application software. A small venture founded by Guy Ravine around the open.ai domain and the 'Open AI' name, and the defendant in OpenAI's trademark action.

status.en: Private; operating status not established in available evidence after July 2025

hq.en: Not disclosed; treated as an evidence gap rather than estimated

prepared_for.en: BSH limited partners and their advisers

text.en: BSH invests in artificial intelligence companies that own something durable: model weights, proprietary data, a technical layer others build on, or a distribution position that compounds. Open Artificial Intelligence, Inc. is a small venture founded by Guy Ravine around the open.ai domain, purchased in March 2015, and…

We are not being offered a priced round, a SAFE, an SPV interest, or a secondary block. There is no instrument, no sponsor, no stated valuation, and no cap table, so there is no entry price to test. That is the central tension: the only asset that ever made this company interesting was a name it is now enjoined from…

items.en: The core bet: any return comes from a legal outcome and a domain disposition, not from an operating business.
The entry tension: there is no price because there is no instrument. Paying less fixes nothing about the situation.
What is proven today: an adverse permanent injunction entered July 21, 2025 against the venture's only identified asset, reported by neutral legal press and by OpenAI's own counsel.
What is missing but modelable: nothing on the revenue side. We model revenue, backlog, and pipeline at zero rather than applying a conversion range to a base that does not exist.
Risk sensitivity: whether the injunction reaches the open.ai domain itself drives essentially all residual value, and that scope is not established in available evidence.
Our action: we do not recommend participating, and we are not participating through any vehicle.

text.en: One point of housekeeping matters more here than in most situations. This entity is not OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. It was the defendant in OpenAI's trademark action, and searches on the name return the plaintiff almost exclusively. Any future evidence of scale, hiring, or partnership that arrives under this…

Guy Ravine bought the open.ai domain in March 2015 and circulated a concept for an open, collaborative, non-profit AI research organization. Yann LeCun has publicly recalled seeing that concept, which makes the early activity real and dated rather than reconstructed. The concept did not become a functioning platform.…

OpenAI sued. On July 21, 2025 Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued a nineteen-page order granting complete summary judgment: a permanent injunction against use of the 'Open AI' name and cancellation of the USPTO registration. The cancellation rested on a fraud finding. User comments submitted to the trademark office as…

What the business actually did is thinly evidenced. The offering the court identified was chatbot and image-generator tools, which is downstream consumption of third-party frontier models rather than ownership of a model, a platform, or infrastructure. No proprietary technology, patent estate, standards position, or…

Everything else is a gap rather than a number. Headquarters, founding year, employee band, capital raised, revenue, customers, partners, and acquisitions are all undisclosed, and we treat each as an evidence gap that flows into the risk register and the scenario weights rather than as a figure to estimate. text.en: The constructive case has four legs, and each deserves to be walked to its end, because the name attached to this company will keep it circulating and a bare rejection would not explain why we stopped.

items.en: Genuine 2015 priority. Ravine bought open.ai in March 2015, months before OpenAI existed, and circulated an open-collaboration research concept that Yann LeCun publicly recalled seeing. The fact is real, dated, and independently attested.
A scarce domain. open.ai is a short category domain in the most valuable software category of the decade, and premium domain value is largely independent of trademark rights.
An unresolved appeal. Counsel signalled an appeal from the July 21, 2025 order, and no appellate outcome is established in available evidence, so the legal position is not final.
Category adjacency. The open, collaborative AI thesis Ravine described in 2015 turned out to be directionally right, which is why the story keeps drawing attention.

text.en: Each leg carries less weight than it first appears. Priority was tested adversarially and lost, because US trademark rights follow use in commerce rather than registration, and the loss itself implies the company could not demonstrate protectable prior use. That inference corroborates the empty adoption record from a…

text.en: Risk here does not concentrate where it usually does. There is no execution risk against a plan, no share loss to defend, and no runway to run out, because none of those things exist in evidence. It concentrates in three places: whether there is anything to buy, whether the one asset that might have survived actually did, and whether anything a counterparty tells us later can be believed.
Risk 1: There is no instrument, no price, and no counterparty, so there is nothing to buy

rows.en: No round, SAFE, SPV interest, secondary block, or term sheet exists in available evidence, and no sponsor, lead, or intermediary is involved. With no stated pre-money and no cap table, no ownership percentage or dilution outcome can be computed for any check size. Valuation support is not weak here; it is absent, which is why a lower price does not improve the case.

A term sheet or subscription document naming an issuer, a security, and a pre-money valuation. An institutional sponsor or intermediary taking the mandate. A stated allocation with defined investor reporting.
High: nothing in available evidence indicates a financing is in market, and no materials dated after July 2025 exist.
10/10: with no instrument there is no investment case to support at any price.

text.en: Risk 2: The July 21, 2025 injunction removed the company's only identified asset

rows.en: The Northern District of California granted complete summary judgment for OpenAI, permanently barred Ravine and the company from using the 'Open AI' name, and ordered the USPTO registration cancelled. The venture's entire distinguishable position was that name and the open.ai domain. Removing the name removes the brand and the customer-acquisition channel at once, and leaves any rebranded entity starting from a null demand base. We carry the mark at zero and treat it as a liability that invites further enforcement exposure.
Any Ninth Circuit ruling on the signalled appeal. The text of the injunction order and whether its scope reaches the open.ai domain. Registrar records showing a change in control of the domain.
High: the order has already been entered and no appellate reversal appears in available evidence.
9/10: it eliminates the asset the entire story rested on.

text.en: Risk 3: The court found the trademark evidence was fabricated, so company-supplied numbers cannot be believed

rows.en: The cancellation rested on a fraud finding. User comments submitted to the trademark office as proof of market traction were planted by an employee of Ravine's, and the court found knowing intent to deceive on clear and convincing evidence. Any traction, traffic, or revenue figure supplied by the company therefore carries no evidentiary weight without independent verification. That permanently discounts the cheapest and fastest evidence a private company can produce, and it makes conviction far more expensive to reach than any plausible position would justify.

Independently verifiable operating evidence such as filed financial statements, a named customer willing to speak, or third-party traffic measurement. Any post-judgment ruling that qualifies or narrows the fraud holding.
High: the finding stands unless an appeal disturbs it, and it applies to every company-originated figure.
9/10: it removes the ordinary path to conviction, not just one datapoint.

text.en: Risk 4: The entity may no longer be operating, and nothing in evidence is dated after July 2025

rows.en: No website, headquarters, employee band, funding, product, or contract is on record, and the freshest dated item is the July 21, 2025 order. That leaves roughly thirteen months to August 24, 2026 with no evidence of operation, financing, appeal progress, or wind-down. Silence is not proof of dormancy, but it is not evidence of activity either, and we will not assume a going concern in order to have something to value. If the entity is dormant, every scenario above the bear case collapses.

A state registry of record showing the entity active, suspended, or dissolved. A live product surface or DNS record at any domain the company controls. Any filing, hire, or public statement dated after July 2025.
Medium: absence of evidence in a thin record is a realistic but unproven indicator of dormancy, and no dissolution filing appears either.
8/10: it decides whether a company exists at all, though one primary check would resolve it.

text.en: Risk 5: Whatever product existed is a wrapper on someone else's models, with no pricing power

rows.en: The offering identified in court was chatbot and image-generator tools running on third-party frontier models. Input costs in that position are set by the model providers, switching costs for users are close to zero, and the competitive set is the entire frontier-lab and open-weight ecosystem. The open, collaborative research niche the 2015 concept aimed at is now held by OpenAI, Hugging Face, and open-weight model communities. We score ecosystem and channel optionality at zero in every scenario.
Evidence of proprietary model weights, data, or infrastructure. A cleared patent search returning a real estate. A named channel, reseller, or cloud-marketplace placement.
High: the application layer above frontier models is abundant and low-barrier, and no differentiating technical evidence exists.
7/10: it caps upside even in the scenarios where the legal position improves.

text.en: Risk 6: The open.ai domain may itself fall inside the injunction, leaving no residual asset

rows.en: An injunction against a mark does not automatically reach a domain, but a domain that functions as a source identifier can fall within such an order. The order's scope on this point is not established in available evidence. This single question drives essentially all residual value: an unencumbered, transferable domain is an asset to sell, and an encumbered one leaves close to nothing. No appraisal or comparable set exists, and premium domain comparables vary by more than an order of magnitude, so we carry the domain at an unquantified value rather than at a point estimate.
The injunction text and any post-judgment order addressing the domain. Registrar and WHOIS records showing who controls open.ai and whether it resolves. Any reported transfer or sale of the domain.
Medium: both outcomes are realistic and the remedy scope is unread.
7/10: it sets the floor value, though on its own it cannot make the position investable.

text.en: What argues against our negative view

items.en: Empty fields are non-disclosure, not audited zero. A private company owes no one a revenue figure, and the record we hold is thin rather than investigated. It is evidence of what has been collected, not of what exists.
The open.ai domain is genuinely scarce, was bought in March 2015, and premium domains hold market value largely independent of trademark rights. Residual value is not strictly zero.
The injunction bars a name, not a company. A rebranded product, a team, or technology could exist outside our line of sight, and losing a trademark says nothing about technical capability.

The July 21, 2025 order is a district-court decision and counsel signalled an appeal. Finality is not established, and no post-judgment procedural history is in evidence, so we carry the legal outcome as an unresolved sensitivity rather than as settled.
No dissolution, solvency, or wind-down filing appears either. Non-operation is unproven in both directions, so our going-concern point is an inference rather than a finding.

Our negative read rests on the same empty record as any positive read, so we hold it with matching humility. The main sources on the ruling are secondary press and a publication of OpenAI's own counsel, and the primary docket has not been read.

text.en: Downside scenario

Our downside is not a lower return; it is a total loss with no recovery mechanism. Assume the entity is dormant, the appeal lapses or fails, and the injunction is read to reach the open.ai domain along with the name. In that state there is no revenue, no team, no transferable asset, and an unquantified legal exposure from an adverse judgment that could exceed anything on the balance sheet. Capital committed into that state does not return at a discount; it returns nothing, and no secondary market or trade-sale route exists to recover it. Because the loss is structural rather than valuation-driven, our recommendation does not move with price, which is the clearest way to see why this is a pass rather than a bid at a lower number.

We publish no valuation range, no forward revenue, and no multiple, because every input on both sides of every ratio is missing. None of the quantitative fields available to us are populated: no capital raised, no revenue, no headcount, no contract value, no valuation mark. Standard fallbacks all fail here.…

Those are different disciplines with different inputs. We would value a confirmed, unencumbered open.ai against premium-domain…
Valuation sensitivities that would move our view

items.en: The largest single swing factor is whether the July 21, 2025 injunction reaches the open.ai domain itself. Order text and registrar records showing the domain unencumbered would move residual value from unquantified to estimable, and it is the only item capable of supporting any price at all.
A Ninth Circuit ruling narrowing or reversing the district court would restore optionality to the mark. Absent that, we carry the mark at zero and treat the story as closed on the brand axis.

One independently verified operating fact dated after July 2025, such as a live product surface, a named customer, or a filed financial statement, would move the revenue line off zero. Company-supplied figures carry no weight given the fraud finding on the trademark specimen, so verification has to come from outside…

A priced round with an institutional sponsor, a stated pre-money, and defined investor reporting would create the first testable entry price. Without one, valuation support is absent at any number, and scarcity of allocation cannot be argued.

Entity status from a state registry of record would resolve whether this is an operating company or a shell. That distinction determines whether the base and bull scenarios have any weight at all, and it is the cheapest evidence with the largest effect on our scenario weights.
A cleared patent and trademark search would establish whether any technical estate exists. We currently model none, so a real estate would be a genuine upward revision rather than a confirmation.
